The Best Principal in the World

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In the middle of rural Limpopo during some of South Africa’s darkest days, why did the Head of a village school get crowned “Best Principal in the World”?

Unique Selling Point:
Dr Ngwako Sebopetsa, the Principal of Rathaga Primary school, doesn't believe in limitations, only in opportunities that one creates for oneself and those around one. He is giving us access to himself, his school, parents and teachers to bear witness to an extraordinary story of hope for our children’s educational future. If this Principal can get great outcomes in rural Limpopo during the pandemic, we must learn and be inspired to spread his approach across all of South Africa. A truly inspirational figure, and a feel good story.

Summary:
Dr Ngwako Sebopetsa has his own motto, "Hard work kills nobody". And he certainly has proved it for himself, with a doctorate in Education management, he has 5 degrees and 5 diplomas to his name. Now he is in pursuit of a Law degree through Unisa. Single-handedly he has made great strides in Education, leaving his mark on the learners of Limpopo. What keeps him motivated is commitment. His secret he says is to ensure that his pupils, teachers and the parents are also committed, this in turn engenders investment by all participants.

And how do you instill that commitment when sometimes if feels impossible? Dr Sebopetsa believes that as individuals we have to leave a mark on society and by leaving our mark, we can change our circumstance and our environment for the better. He is living proof of this dictum. In one of his previous schools he raised the pass rate from 25% to 75%. At his current Rathaga Primary School the learner enrollment has risen from about 550 to more than 800 in the last 5 years.

Dr Sebopetsa has a unique and committed style which is bringing results. So much so that now the Department of Education has asked him to bring some of his learnings and ideas to other schools.


Further information:
Talking to him, one feels Dr Sebopetsa’s passion and his dogged determination to be part of a solution. He identifies that some of his biggest challenges lie within poor communication, lack of resources, de-motivation and high levels of illiteracy with the parents of the students in rural areas. But rural Limpopo is where he was born and bred, and that hasn't stopped him from achieving. In his motivational talks with his students he reinforces that coming from a rural or poor background should not stop them from achieving their goals and dreams. Although he focuses his time on motivating his students and teachers, he believes that parents are part and parcel of this process of ensuring such positive growth, an example he has learnt from his own father, a teacher too and an inspiration for him.

Understanding the challenges of his environment Dr Sebopetsa even incentivises parents to make the trek, sometimes risking their well being, to participate in school activities and become part of their children's education. He believes their involvement is so crucial for their children’s education that he gets sponsorship from the local stores and at times even reaches into his own pocket, to organise groceries or hampers as give-aways for parents who make an extra effort to participate. He uses trusted business principles within the school context.

After talking with Dr Sebopetsa, he has invited us to his school so we can learn more about this extraordinary man and his environment. He also says we can film around the school and interview learners, teachers and parents to hear what they have to say - how Dr Sebopetsa inspires them to be extra-committed to their children's education.

Press Release:


Being a recipient of the Global principals’ award is a tall order. And when that principal is head of a primary school in rural Limpopo, one wonders, what is his secret ingredient and what lessons should we be learning from Dr Sebopetsa?

Script:


VO: Deep rural Limpopo, isolated from the trimmings of urban wealth and amenities. Here in Mapone District at Rathaga Primary school, one man is making his mark - One child, one teacher, one parent at a time.

Michael: He's the first one to arrive at school. The last one to leave.

VO: Meet Principal Dr Ngwako Sebopetsa

Dr Sebopetsa: I remember when my father was a principal, he said my son, go out. The world doesn't owe you anything. don't expect to become a millionaire, go and change the world, and I did,

Millicent: He's the second father to my son, our children are safe. They are in good hands when they are here at Rathaga.

VO: Dr Ngwako Sebopetsa, is showing the way. Through his efforts, Rathaga Primary has become so popular that enrolment increased from 500 to 800 learners, and in his previous posts his results were no less astounding

Dr Sebopetsa: A School was performing below 30% for the past five years, They placed me for a period of two years, they saidwant to see. The first year it rocketed from 30% to 65. The following year from 65 to 75%. // Which means that it is possible. Commitment, It must not be taught. It must be seen

VO: It’s a testament to his personal motto, hard work kills nobody.

Dr Sebopetsa: This motto propelled me to move in difficult situations *I'm coming from the deep rural part of of Limpopo, but my background does not determine my destination.. Through Hard work. Nothing's impossible. It might be difficult at that time, but the fruits you are going to enjoy.

VO: And after 30 years as an educator he's borne the fruits of his efforts, becoming a winner of the 2020 global principals’ award.

Dr Sebopetsa: When they read my name, I couldn't believe my ears and eyes. Yoh I jumped. I even went out take water and pour my face where if I'm dreaming or not,
Masa: You competed with some of the best schools all over the world from a village school?
Dr Sebopetsa: This competition is unique,it does not consider the infrastructure.They want what the principal is doing in order to change the school, how it affects the community, and also the parents.

VO: Being recognised as one of the best performers in education is high praise, so what is the secret behind his success?

Dr Sebopetsa: Sound up: My message is, how to take charge of our lives.
Dr Sebopetsa: You need to understand your role and responsibility as a principal and as a leader. you are the engine of the school, You will need to have an innovative mind of where are you going to take the school,

Dr Sebopetsa sound up: No great achievement is possible without persistent work.

Michael: If you motivate your teachers then the result that will be shown by the performance of the learners.

VO: Well aware of the challenges this principal faces is Michael Motloutsi, a parent who has served twice as chairperson of the School governing body.

Michael: Some of the child are orphans, some are travelling more than eight kilometres here. They travel on foot.

VO: Despite these difficulties 13 year old Lethabo Sethaba finds her school environment a source of motivation.

Lethabo: The principal is the one who helped me with the uniform, the books and pens, and encouraged me to study, and I will achieve my goal.
Masa: Doesn't matter your background?
Lethabo: The situation of today is not the situation of tomorrow.

VO: Striving to steer these young minds towards a better tomorrow are teachers like Reverend Rachel Motloutsi.

Rachel: My teaching style has changed. The spirit of laziness, the spirit of being in a comfort zone has changed. Like when it is raining, you know children will come in wet and you have to, comfort them and make ways for them to listen to you even you see that it is not easy.

Michael: Some of them sleep on, on an empty stomach, And they don't do well at school because they're hungry.

VO: A plate of food at school is a necessity for some, but during the pandemic classes are rotated, so those who aren't at school may end up going hungry. But through donations Dr Sebopetsa makes a plan for extra food during the week and for weekends.

Dr Sebopetsa: Even though they are not expected to come for that day, they will come in for food. And this has proved that the learner absenteeism it's no longer there because they know that our school, it's a kitchen for everybody.

VO: Even if the challenges are poverty and illiteracy he insists that parents must play an active role in their children's education.

Dr Sebopetsa: Parents were reluctant to come to meetings. On my own, I pop out, buy some soap, buy some toiletries, the first ten parents who come to school, during meetings, they're given those things.

Michael: Some years back, he got a donation from the Australian embassy. They got a huge tank, the school never struggled with water

VO: And at age 60, with 5 degrees and 5 diplomas, he's now chasing a Law Degree. So one would think that with an entire school to take care of and four children of his own he couldn't take on much more.

Dr Sebopetsa: I've got two girls that I've adopted. They're my children. When they're in grade 12 I will assist them so that they go to institutions of higher learning. I want to see them better in life.

LINK: It's one thing to have a belief system of commitment and hard work as Dr. Ngwako Sebopetsa has proved through his life achievements, but it's another to get other people to follow in your footsteps.

VO: So Rathaga Primary also facilitates centres of learning and Parent to 10 year old Kelebogile, Millicent Ramalepe is reaping the benefits of his mentorship.

Millicent: You are never too old to get educated. I was doing my diploma in policing,because that's where I'm working. So this year I graduated because he inspired me to go back to school.

Rachel: I worked with other principals, But when it comes to Dr. Sebopetsa, he is wonderful. And he would always say to the children, "Rathaga is always number one" .
Dr Sebopetsa Sound up: Rathaga is always number one

VO: And Rathaga certainly beat the odds with learners winning national competitions, even in artistic gymnastics for rope skipping.

Masa: Do you have a gymnasium?
Dr Sebopetsa: We just use the classroom. Imagine, If the infrastructure was good, we're going to get stars here.

LINK: With a 70% unemployment rate amongst the youth, a pandemic and an economy that's not about to recover anytime soon. How does one man teach others to leave their mark?

Dr Sebopetsa: All these things that we see here is temporary. the youth that we see in front of us now, they're not going to be youth forever. Let's see the world in different eyes. Our system makes our graduates to rely much on government, instead of creating jobs for ourselves.

VO: This principal is intent on impacting his community to leave behind a legacy of hope.

Rachel: He's taking most of the things on his shoulders. His father encouraged him to be a hard worker, then but I think he's working more.

Dr Sebopetsa: I will ask God that give me 36 hours in a day. Unfortunately, it is not possible. It's 24 hours, If you waste it, it can't come again. //
That's why I talk of hard work kills nobody //
and it worked for me.

At his current Rathaga Primary School the learner enrollment has risen from about 550 to more than 800 in the last 5 years. Dr Sebopetsa has a unique and committed style which is bringing results. So much so that now the Department of Education has asked him to bring some of his learnings and ideas to other schools.
metadata.Further information: Talking to him, one feels Dr Sebopetsa’s passion and his dogged determination to be part of a solution. He identifies that some of his biggest challenges lie within poor communication, lack of resources, de-motivation and high levels of illiteracy with the parents of the students in rural areas. But rural Limpopo is where he was born and bred, and that hasn't stopped him from achieving. In his motivational talks with his students he reinforces that coming from a rural or poor background should not stop them from achieving their goals and dreams. Although he focuses his time on motivating his students and teachers, he believes that parents are part and parcel of this process of ensuring such positive growth, an example he has learnt from his own father, a teacher too and an inspiration for him. Understanding the challenges of his environment Dr Sebopetsa even incentivises parents to make the trek, sometimes risking their well being, to participate in school activities and become part of their children's education. He believes their involvement is so crucial for their children’s education that he gets sponsorship from the local stores and at times even reaches into his own pocket, to organise groceries or hampers as give-aways for parents who make an extra effort to participate. He uses trusted business principles within the school context. After talking with Dr Sebopetsa, he has invited us to his school so we can learn more about this extraordinary man and his environment. He also says we can film around the school and interview learners, teachers and parents to hear what they have to say - how Dr Sebopetsa inspires them to be extra-committed to their children's education.
